sections.h2: Where is Floyd County and what is the land like?
sections.html:
Floyd County is a small county on the Ohio River, directly across from Louisville, Kentucky. It covers about 149 square miles, which makes it the second-smallest county in Indiana by area. Only Ohio County is smaller. New Albany is both the county seat and the largest city, and the county belongs to the Louisville and Jefferson County metropolitan area.

The river forms the southern boundary and holds the county's lowest point, 380 feet above sea level near New Albany. Part of the county sits in the Knobs, one of the hilliest parts of Indiana, with dry ridgetops and wet ravines. Clark, Harrison and Washington counties lie to the northeast, west and northwest. Floyds Knobs and Edwardsville are two named places outside the city. The county has five townships and nine public parks, the largest being the 104-acre Sam Peden Community Park.

sections.h2: What is New Albany's history, and why does it matter for sellers?
sections.html:
New Albany was once the largest city in Indiana, and its old building stock shows it. Three Scribner brothers from New York founded the town in July 1813. The city held the top spot from 1816 until 1860, when Indianapolis passed it.

Shipbuilding and steamboats drove the early economy, and the steamboat trade ended by 1870. American Plate Glass Works opened in 1865 and employed up to 2,000 people before moving in 1893. Plywood and veneer manufacturing came next. The Scribner House, built in 1814, still stands, and Main Street holds late 19th century mansions from the shipbuilding years.

The Culbertson Mansion, a French Second Empire home, is now an Indiana state memorial, and the Town Clock Church was a stop on the Underground Railroad. Older homes near downtown share the area with newer subdivisions toward the I-265 corridor, so condition and age vary a lot from one block to the next.

Income data shows why some owners fall behind. The 2023 median household income in New Albany was $54,152, against $69,477 statewide, and the poverty rate was 18.4%, against 12.3% for Indiana.

sections.h2: What flood and storm history should Floyd County sellers know?
sections.html:
Floyd County's biggest weather risk is the Ohio River. In January 1937 the river reached 60.8 feet at New Albany, and most of the town stood under water for nearly three weeks. Afterward New Albany became the first city in the region to build flood walls, and Louisville and Clark County later used its walls as models.

A tornado on March 23, 1917 killed at least 46 people on the north side of the city. The Knobs bring their own terrain, with dry ridgetops and wet ravines, so a hillside lot deserves a close look at drainage before you list.

  • Ask your insurer whether the parcel is in a mapped flood zone before you list.
  • Keep repair records for any basement or foundation water work.
  • Expect buyers to ask about roof age on older New Albany houses.

sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Floyd County?
sections.html:
Three offices share the work, and all three are in New Albany. The treasurer collects, the assessor values and the auditor handles rates, calculations and deduction forms. The county's pages show one address problem that sellers should know: the treasurer's page lists both 120 West Spring Street, Suite 201 and 311 Hauss Square, Room 113 for in-person payments. Call before you drive over.

The treasurer takes payment in several ways. Online payments go through floydcountyintax.com. Phone payments cost $0.65 by e-check or 2.25% by card. Mail goes to PO Box 3697, Evansville, IN 47736, and it must be postmarked by the due date. A 24-hour drop box is available, and German American Bank accepts payments at any Floyd County branch. First Harrison Bank and Stock Yards Bank no longer do. A bill reprint costs $1.

The assessor's office also handles property transfers and splits, new construction, sales disclosures and the plat room. The auditor's page links the homestead, over 65 and mortgage deduction forms on the state's site.

sections.h2: How does Floyd County value a house?
sections.html:
Tyler Technologies prepared Floyd County's 2025 ratio study, which tests how close assessed values come to sale prices. The study used sales from January 1 to December 31, 2024. It describes sales as strong in the first half of 2024 and slower in the second half, with prices staying high. New construction rose.

  • Overall values increased across the county.
  • Residential, commercial and industrial improved values rose because of cost table updates, trending changes and more new construction.
  • In that phase of reassessment, only sections of Lafayette and New Albany townships were reviewed, against a target of 25% of parcels with a 2% tolerance.
  • Where a neighborhood had too few sales, it was combined with a neighbor that has similar economics.
  • A land order went to the county board on February 4, 2025 and took effect that day.

Form 11, the notice of assessment, is mailed by April 30 each year. The assessor's page says appeals are due June 15 on Form 130, and the county appeals board lists three members. An error such as a removed garage or wrong square footage can be corrected on page 1 and section III of page 2 of the same form.

sections.h2: How do tax caps and appeals work for a Floyd County seller?
sections.html:
The state caps tax at 1% of gross assessed value for a homestead and 2% for other residential property and farmland. Nonresidential property and personal property are capped at 3%. You need the homestead standard deduction to get the 1% cap, and the homestead covers the house, a garage and up to one acre.

The appeal process runs on state timelines. After you file Form 130, the assessor meets with you informally, and the appeals board must hold a hearing within 180 days. You get at least 30 days of written notice. A written continuance request is due 10 days before the hearing. If the board disagrees with you or does not decide in 180 days, you can take the case to the Indiana Board of Tax Review on Form 131.

If you appeal, you may pay on last year's assessment while the case is pending. Paying less than that amount makes the installment delinquent, and penalties apply.

sections.h2: What happens in a Floyd County tax sale?
sections.html:
A county tax sale offers parcels with delinquent taxes to bidders. The treasurer's page describes Floyd County's sale as fully online. Bidders register at sriservices.com, and parcel details are on lowtaxinfo.com/floydcounty. The page gives October 15, 2026 as the sale date.

An owner who wants a parcel off the list has to pay the treasurer directly. For parcels eligible for the sale, the page says online and credit card payments are not accepted, so payment must be cash in exact change or certified funds. The auditor's page lists tax sale notices, tax sale appeals, records of sale and deeds.

The state penalty rules show how the debt grows before a sale. A late payment draws 5% if made within 30 days and no earlier delinquency exists, and 10% in other cases. A later installment date adds another 10% of the unpaid principal. Payments are applied to the tax first and penalties second. A seller who closes before the sale date normally clears the whole amount through the title company.

sections.h2: What do roads, schools and local services look like?
sections.html:
Floyd County's road network ties into Louisville. I-265 forms the northern edge of New Albany, and I-64 was built through the city in 1961, which led to the Sherman Minton Bridge. A rail and road link to Kentucky opened in 1886. Highway 150 runs near Mount Saint Francis in Floyds Knobs.

The New Albany-Floyd County Consolidated School Corporation runs the public schools. New Albany High School opened in 1853 as the state's first public high school. Indiana University Southeast sits on the northern edge of the city, and the Duncan Tunnel, finished in 1881 between New Albany and Edwardsville, is the longest in Indiana at 4,311 feet.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Floyd County?
faqs.a: The Floyd County Treasurer collects it, and the office is in New Albany. Call (812) 948-5477, option 4 for tax payments, to confirm the right address first.

faqs.q: When is the appeal deadline in Floyd County?
faqs.a: June 15, on Form 130 filed with the Floyd County Assessor. Notices of assessment are mailed by April 30.

faqs.q: Can a Floyd County house be sold with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company pays the back tax and penalties from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the treasurer for the current balance so you know what to expect.

faqs.q: How much is the late penalty in Floyd County?
faqs.a: It is 5% if you pay within 30 days of the due date and have no earlier delinquency, and 10% in other cases. State law adds another 10% of the unpaid tax at later installment dates.

faqs.q: Does the Ohio River affect selling a house in Floyd County?
faqs.a: It can. The river forms the county's southern edge and flooded most of New Albany in 1937. A buyer or lender may ask about flood zone status and insurance for homes near the water.
